analysis.one_liner: Caps federal spending at a falling share of the economy and blocks new borrowing until a balanced budget amendment passes.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill; with no cosponsors, it sat on the Senate calendar from October 2015 until the Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set a hard ceiling on federal spending for fiscal 2016 — about $2.88 trillion in outlays — and then cap total spending at a shrinking share of the economy, from 19.9% down to 18% over ten years. Spending that exceeds the caps would be cut automatically. Social Security, Medicare, veterans' benefits, military personnel, and interest on the debt would be exempt, so the cuts would fall on everything else: education, transportation, health research, food safety, Medicaid, and other programs. It would also block the Treasury from using any additional borrowing authority until Congress sends the states a constitutional amendment requiring a balanced budget, a spending cap, and a two-thirds vote in both chambers for any tax increase.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthier households benefit from the two-thirds supermajority requirement for tax increases, which would make raising taxes on any income group extremely difficult. Defense is protected: military pay is exempt from the caps and budget committee chairs could add up to $58 billion for war-related spending. Social Security and Medicare beneficiaries are shielded from the automatic cuts. Supporters also argue that restraining the deficit benefits the whole economy over time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy households, defense, and large entitlement programs

how_it_helps.text: The bill caps total federal spending at 19.9% of GDP in fiscal 2016, declining to 18% by fiscal 2021 through 2025, enforcing the cap with automatic spending cuts, which supporters present as a way to shrink deficits and debt.
Social Security, Medicare, veterans' benefits, net interest, and military personnel accounts are exempt from the spending limits, so the largest and most popular programs would be spared the cuts.
Budget committee chairs could raise the limits by up to $58 billion for spending designated for overseas contingency operations, giving defense-related spending a protected escape valve.

The bill bars the Treasury from exercising additional borrowing authority until a balanced budget amendment is transmitted to the states — one that requires outlays not exceed receipts, caps spending as a share of GDP, and requires a two-thirds vote in both houses for tax increases.

analysis.who_pays: Programs not on the exemption list — Medicaid, food assistance, education, transportation, scientific research, food safety, and other domestic programs — would bear the full weight of automatic sequestration cuts. Ordinary people who use those services would lose them or see them degrade. The borrowing block also raises the risk of a payments crisis if new borrowing authority is ever needed.

drawbacks.text: Because the largest programs are exempt, the automatic sequestration cuts would be concentrated on nonexempt domestic programs such as Medicaid, education, transportation, and research, hitting services ordinary people rely on.

The requirement that tax increases pass with a two-thirds vote in both chambers, once the constitutional amendment is transmitted, would make it far harder to raise revenue in any future fiscal emergency.

The bill blocks the Treasury from using any additional borrowing authority until a balanced budget amendment is sent to the states, which could leave the government unable to pay its bills if the amendment stalled.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pursues a real public goal — bringing deficits and debt under control — but its design shifts nearly the entire burden onto the programs left outside the exemptions, while carving out defense, large entitlements, and interest payments. The two-thirds requirement for tax increases makes the adjustment one-sided: spending shrinks but revenue cannot rise. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the caps as written would force deep cuts to domestic programs while exempting most of the budget.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Paul introduced it in October 2015, it was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar, and with no cosponsors and no committee action it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2017 without ever coming to a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Rand Paul introduced S. 2182 in the Senate on October 19, 2015, where it was read the first time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under Read the First Time.
The next day it was read a second time and placed on the Senate calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 274) — the list of bills awaiting floor action.
The bill drew no cosponsors in the Senate.
No committee considered the bill and no vote was ever held; the Congress ended on January 3, 2017 with the bill still on the calendar.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed, so the people who use nonexempt federal programs were spared the automatic cuts the bill would have imposed, and defense and large entitlement programs kept their current funding. Wealthy households and other taxpayers continued to face tax policy set by ordinary majority rules rather than the bill's two-thirds requirement.

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar; no other senator joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote or committee action; it sat on the calendar for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. The only sign of support was the Republican sponsor himself, with zero cosponsors from either party, so the partisan shape of the bill never got tested.

industries.note: Military personnel accounts are exempt from all spending limits, and budget chairs could adjust the caps by up to $58 billion for overseas war spending, shielding defense while other programs absorb cuts.

industries.industry: Wealthiest households and other high taxpayers
industries.note: The bill conditions new borrowing on a constitutional amendment requiring a two-thirds vote in both chambers for any tax increase, making it much harder to raise taxes on high earners even during fiscal emergencies.

industries.industry: Nonexempt domestic programs and their contractors and grantees (education, transportation, research, food safety, Medicaid)
industries.note: With the largest programs exempt, automatic sequestration cuts would fall on these programs, reducing funding for services ordinary people use and for the organizations that provide them.
